title: Whipple Disease
subject: Medicine
summary: A rare systemic infection by Tropheryma whipplei presenting with malabsorption, arthralgia, and neurological signs. Diagnosis relies on PAS‑positive macrophages or PCR; treatment is prolonged antibiotics.

sections.p: Whipple disease is a chronic infection caused by the gram‑positive actinomycete Tropheryma whipplei. It is characterised by foamy macrophages laden with PAS‑positive material in the lamina propria of the small intestine and other tissues.
b: Often misdiagnosed as tropical sprue or celiac disease

t.b: Shows PAS‑positive foamy macrophages in lamina propria; confirms tissue involvement
Gold standard; detects bacterial DNA in biopsy, CSF or blood when biopsy unavailable
Adjunctive; positive in many but not specific; useful when PCR not available

sections.p: Patients are staged by organ involvement: gastrointestinal (malabsorption), rheumatologic (arthralgia), neurological (meningoencephalitis), and cardiac (valvulitis).

t.b: Elevated protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis suggest CNS disease
Detects valvular thickening or regurgitation indicating cardiac involvement

sections.p: The primary cause is infection with T. whipplei, acquired via ingestion or inhalation. In low‑resource settings, co‑infection with HIV or malnutrition may worsen presentation.
b: Concurrent TB or malaria may mask symptoms

t.b: Rule out immunosuppression that can mimic or worsen disease
Low albumin may mimic protein‑losing enteropathy

sections.p: Patients report chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, abdominal pain, and low‑grade fever. Arthralgia is common, often migratory. Neurological signs appear late: tremor, gait disturbance, or confusion.

t.b: Look for cachexia, joint swelling, neurological deficits

sections.p: Investigation strategy prioritises tests that are affordable in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Rule out bacterial causes of diarrhoea; negative in Whipple
Confirms diagnosis when biopsy is not feasible

sections.p: Untreated disease leads to irreversible neurological damage, heart failure, and death. Early recognition of CNS or cardiac involvement is critical.
Long‑term antibiotic therapy is curative. First‑line is a combination of a beta‑lactam and a macrolide to penetrate the CNS.

t.b: Alternative for patients with beta‑lactam allergy; good CNS penetration

sections.p: Patients require 12–18 months of therapy and regular monitoring for relapse. Prevention focuses on early diagnosis and treatment of co‑existing infections.
b: Monthly clinical review for first 6 months

sections.p: Tropical sprue, celiac disease, and protein‑losing enteropathy share similar GI symptoms.
b: Tropical sprue – responds to antibiotics but lacks PAS‑positive macrophages

t.b: Positive IgA TTG suggests celiac, not Whipple

sections.p: PAS staining may be weak; PCR may be negative if sampling is inadequate.
b: False‑negative biopsy if only mucosa sampled

faq.q: Why is PCR preferred over culture?
faq.a: T. whipplei is difficult to culture; PCR detects bacterial DNA directly.

faq.q: Can Whipple disease be cured with a short course of antibiotics?
faq.a: No, treatment must be prolonged (12–18 months) to eradicate the organism from all tissues.

faq.q: What is the role of doxycycline?
faq.a: It is used when patients cannot tolerate beta‑lactams and provides good CNS penetration.

exam: A 35‑year‑old man with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss presents with new tremor. What is the next best investigation? — CSF analysis to rule out CNS involvement.
A patient with suspected Whipple disease has a negative small bowel biopsy. What should you do next? — Perform PCR for T. whipplei on biopsy or blood.
Why is ceftriaxone chosen as initial therapy? — It penetrates the CNS and is bactericidal against T. whipplei.
A patient with HIV develops arthralgia and diarrhoea. How do you differentiate Whipple disease from HIV‑related enteropathy? — Look for PAS‑positive macrophages or PCR positivity.
What complication is most feared if CNS disease is untreated? — Progressive dementia and seizures.
A patient on long‑term antibiotics develops a rash. Which drug is most likely responsible? — Doxycycline can cause photosensitivity.
